title: PAIGE: Examining Learning Outcomes and Experiences with Personalized AI-Generated Educational Podcasts
extended_summary:
This preprint investigates whether generative AI can transform textbook chapters into educational podcasts that are both engaging and effective for learning, and whether personalization improves outcomes further. The authors focus on two main questions: how students perceive AI-generated podcasts compared with traditional textbook reading, and whether generalized versus personalized podcasts affect learning outcomes differently across subject areas.

The intervention was a system called PAIGE, which converts OpenStax textbook chapters into AI-generated educational podcasts using Gemini 1.5 Pro for transcript generation and a text-to-speech voice model based on AudioLM for spoken delivery. Personalized podcasts were tailored using learner profile data collected before the study, including students’ major, age group, interests, and preferred learning style. The study compared three conditions: traditional textbook reading, generalized AI-generated podcasts, and personalized AI-generated podcasts.

The study involved 180 current college students in the United States, recruited through Prolific, with participants randomly assigned across a 3x3 design spanning three college textbook subjects: philosophy, psychology, and American government. Each participant completed a single 35-minute remote online session that included exposure to one learning condition, a user experience questionnaire, a 10-item objective multiple-choice knowledge test drawn from textbook test banks, and free-response feedback. This provided both quantitative and qualitative data about learning and experience.

The main conclusions are that AI-generated podcasts were rated as more attractive/enjoyable than textbooks, regardless of whether they were personalized. Personalized podcasts improved learning outcomes in some subjects—especially philosophy, and to a lesser extent psychology—but not in government, suggesting that the effectiveness of personalization depends on how well the personalized context meaningfully connects to the subject matter. The authors conclude that AI-generated podcasts are a promising modality for making textbook content more engaging, but that personalization should be applied carefully and evaluated by subject and learner context.

identified_tools.name: PAIGE
identified_tools.description: A research system for converting textbook chapters into AI-generated educational podcasts, with optional personalization using learner profile data such as major, interests, age group, and preferred learning style.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate generalized and personalized educational podcasts from OpenStax textbook chapters for a 3x3 user study comparing podcast-based learning against textbook reading among U.S. college students.

findings.finding_summary: In a user study with 180 U.S. college students, learning outcomes varied by subject, with a significant interaction between content style and subject for test score, F(4,171)=2.27, p<0.01. For Philosophy, the Personalized podcast condition scored significantly higher (M=7.30, SD=1.45) than both the Generalized condition (M=5.85, SD=1.35, p<0.01) and the Textbook condition (M=5.95, SD=1.57, p=0.01); for Psychology there was a significant main effect of content style, F(2,57)=3.17, p=0.04, but no significant pairwise differences, with Personalized trending higher than Generalized (p=0.07) and Textbook (p=0.09); for Government there was no significant main effect, F(2,57)=2.96, p=0.06.
findings.measure: Knowledge retention via 10-item multiple-choice chapter test (scores 0-10)
findings.effect_size: F(4,171)=2.27; Philosophy: F(2,57)=6.14; Psychology: F(2,57)=3.17; Government: F(2,57)=2.96

findings.finding_summary: The AI-generated podcast conditions were rated as more attractive than textbooks on the UEQ Attractiveness scale, with a significant main effect of content style, F(2,171)=11.06, p<0.01. Both Personalized (M=5.25, SD=1.06) and Generalized (M=5.25, SD=0.88) podcasts were rated significantly higher than the Textbook condition (M=4.52, SD=1.03), with no significant interaction by subject.

There were no significant main effects or interaction effects of content style or subject on the UEQ Stimulation scale. Although stimulation ratings showed similar trends to attractiveness, the differences were not statistically significant.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's large language model family used for generating text content from prompts and contextual inputs.
identified_tools.use_case: Gemini 1.5 Pro was used within the PAIGE pipeline to generate podcast configuration files, outlines, and full transcripts from textbook chapters and learner profile information for generalized and personalized educational podcasts.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative experiment with random assignment across conditions and a moderate sample (n=180), but it is an exploratory user study rather than a fully reported RCT with effect sizes and full credibility details.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant benefits for attractiveness and subject-specific learning gains, but effects are mixed across subjects and standardized effect sizes are not reported, making overall impact promising but unclear in magnitude.
